title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You take the lot without a word and keep going like that for months. Your body starts to complain. Your manager assumes you are fine, offers no extra help or anything in return, and treats this as the new normal. Carrying it all is wearing down your health and your position to negotiate.

options.text: Stop in time, and negotiate a sustainable workload and a fair return
Keep carrying until your health goes

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
situation: You have been in an engineering role for years, and you have reached a crossroads. Your manager sits you down: the company can keep you on the technical-expert track, or move you into leading a team. What do you actually want? This will shape a long stretch of your career, so it deserves a proper answer.

options.text: Weigh your interests, strengths and the long-term prospects of both paths before you choose
Hear that management pays more and comes with people reporting to you, and pick it without thinking
Dodge the choice and say you are happy either way, whatever the company prefers

title: Your partner's job offer in another city: live apart, stay, or rethink
situation: You find the nerve to talk to your manager about an internal move or remote working. The company does have a team in that city, but the role does not quite match your current direction. Going would mean proving yourself again and would slow promotion in the short term. What you and your partner both care about is being together.

options.text: Take the move as a fresh start that broadens your CV
The terms of the move do not work, so stay and put up with the travel

title: The company goes all-in on a new bet and sidelines your work
situation: You spread a story you know is untrue, single people out, and get in the way of the new team's delivery. Word reaches leadership, and they mark you down as someone disrupting the work. A plainly stated technical objection would not have done that. Even if the new direction has real problems, you are now first in line to be dropped when the company changes course.

options.text: Drop the attitude, give the new work a fair look and get involved
Keep spreading the untrue story and blocking delivery

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
situation: One sentence stops Lou in her tracks. She goes red, barely speaks to you for days, and tells other people you are 'quite fierce'. You held the line, but a new colleague was rattled and her settling in took a knock.

options.text: Find a moment to soften it: you just don't discuss your private life, and it wasn't personal
Don't soften it. The boundary matters more than her feelings

title: Palpitations after weeks of overtime: whether to stop
situation: Two weeks of late nights. Tonight your heart races, your chest feels tight, and your hands shake. These are clear warning signs, but the task is almost done.

options.text: Stop now, rest, see a doctor if needed, and work at a steadier pace from tomorrow
Drink some water, wait it out, and grind through to the end

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: Faye is touched but still hesitates: 'I feel bad, you've got your own work.' You take the most urgent part and she goes home. Now your own schedule is packed, the milestone is close, and you are feeling the strain.

options.text: Tell your manager you are covering Faye for now, and ask for a realistic plan
Carry all of it without telling anyone, and work late to catch up

title: A Glassdoor post about the company is doing the rounds
situation: A tell-all post about the company is spreading fast on Glassdoor, and only half of it is true. People in the team channel are forwarding it and stirring things up, and they ask what you think.

options.text: Don't spread it or take sides, and pay attention only to facts that affect you
Forward it eagerly to every chat, adding your own embellishments
Leave an anonymous comment adding more detail

title: Your manager gives you a rise — with a lot more work attached
situation: Your manager offers you a rise, then adds, 'Now that the pay is up, you can take on these extra bits of the business as well.' The increase is real, and so is the extra load. The two may not balance.

options.text: Weigh the extra work against the increase, take what is fair, and say so if it would overload you
Get carried away by the rise and accept every new piece of work without counting the load
Take the rise but quietly dodge the extra work

title: Choosing a path for a legacy service hitting its limits
situation: A core order service you own has been live for three years and is reaching its performance limit. Monitoring shows QPS already at 80% of the original design limit, and in another quarter or two normal growth will probably overwhelm it. Your manager has given you three months to propose a path, without saying which one. You could rewrite it on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation,

options.text: Rewrite on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation
Refactor in stages on the current architecture
Ship the smallest performance patches and ride out this cycle

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
situation: The company is setting up a new real-time compute platform, and your manager has put you in charge of the technology choice for your part of it. There are two options. You can build the kernel in-house, which fits the business but means a long build and a painful go-live. Or you can adopt a well-known open-source project, which lets you deliver quickly but leaves the kernel a black box and you at

options.text: Argue for an in-house kernel as a long-term technical asset
Adopt the open-source stack and aim for fast delivery

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
situation: You keep retrying. Five or six minutes of dead air pass, the client's people start looking at their phones, and the room turns icy. A colleague slides you a note: 'Talk about something else first.' The demo has lost all momentum.

options.text: Change tack at once: skip the broken step, talk about overall value, and demo it afterwards
Keep hammering at the bug until time runs out

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
situation: Your friend feels shut out: 'So you're at a level we don't get to now.' Three months later their team is restructured. They feel they could have prepared if they had known earlier, and the friendship cracks.

options.text: Explain that confidentiality is a professional duty. You care about them, but you still cannot share
Don't explain. Accept that work relationships sometimes need this distance

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
situation: You make your case with a solid summary of what you have delivered and a plan for what you will contribute next. Your manager accepts that you are capable, but says the others are strong too and there is a balance to strike. Then you hear a rival has been talking you down behind your back.

options.text: Do not hit back: keep letting your results speak, and set the record straight if needed without attacking them
Get angry, and start talking them down in return

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
situation: An open-source project you run in your own time unexpectedly takes off and starts to bring in consulting income. It is in the same field as the company but aimed at different customers. You have not used company time or kit. Then a client asks whether you also offer enterprise services, which would compete directly with the company.

options.text: Tell your manager and compliance now, and ask them to assess the boundary
Decline the enterprise work, keep the side project community-only, and do not tell the company yet

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
situation: You have watched this for three years. The fastest riser is Harvey: average technically, but he never misses karaoke, five-a-side or the pub after work. Your technical scores have topped the team for years, yet your promotion still lags. Chris says they also look at “the whole picture”.

options.text: Make more effort socially, without crossing your own lines
Refuse to play along and double down on technical output
Tell Helen, the HR business partner, that the promotion criteria are too vague
Start looking elsewhere and ease off here

title: Building a safety net while pay and energy still allow it
situation: You realise your career will not always go this well. While your pay and energy are still decent, you start thinking about building a buffer: savings, a second skill or a network.

options.text: Plan it: build an emergency fund and steadily strengthen one transferable skill
Let anxiety take over: save and study everything at once, and run yourself into the ground
Decide you are overthinking it. Enjoy the present and prepare nothing

title: Build a second curve, or stay focused on the day job?
situation: You want a 'second curve' for the longer term: a new technical direction, some open source, or writing up what you know properly. It will take your evenings, and handled badly it could hurt the day job. How do you balance it?

options.text: Pick a second curve that sits alongside your career, and keep investing without letting the day job slip
Dabble on and off, trying everything and finishing nothing
Dive into the side work and let the day job go to seed

title: A fast-learning new hire stealing the limelight
situation: The new joiner is full of energy, picks things up fast, and came in on a lower salary band. They have run a few meetings well. You can feel people comparing them with you in your more senior, more expensive role.

options.text: Set yourself apart: focus on architecture, quality and the hard problems the new joiner cannot yet handle
Compete on hours and volume to prove you can keep up
Feel sour, quietly freeze them out, and be unhelpful

title: Stuck on repetitive work: do you look for something meatier?
situation: For a long time your work has been low-value and repetitive. It is steady, but it does not stretch you, and if you stay on it your skills will stall. Do you ask for work with more technical substance, something that would actually make you better?

options.text: Ask your manager for harder work, or find a way to make the repetitive work itself more efficient
Keep the repetitive work because it is easy and does not take much thinking
Treat the work as beneath you and phone in even the repetitive jobs

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: You only talked about highlights, and the execs came away impressed on the day. Two months later the risk materialises, the damage spreads, and leadership digs out the briefing notes: 'Why was there not a word about risk?' You are on the back foot.

options.text: Run a review, own the bad call, and show the fix already in place
Argue that 'nobody could have seen this then'

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: Your manager listens and says, 'Noted.' The list comes out and you are going. Jo takes the day off and is noticeably cooler with you afterwards. When you get back, your manager wants you to give the team a 30-minute talk on the conference.

options.text: Thank Jo in the talk for her earlier groundwork, then go and speak to her afterwards
Keep the talk on what you got out of it and reinforce your manager's good impression

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You are working with a remote client entirely over video and chat. After the first delivery they say on a call, “This isn’t what I wanted.” Your chat history shows they had informally agreed to that direction. Reworking it will be expensive, and the team is already grumbling. Their tone on the call is getting sharp.

options.text: Skip the blame game: work out the mismatch and propose prototypes or visual specs before building more
Pull up the chat log and argue that they already confirmed it
Rework the lot without question, doing whatever they say

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
situation: You wait and commit to nobody. Once the integration settles you have neither joined the new organisation nor stayed with the old camp, and neither side counts you as one of theirs.

options.text: Pick a direction, join the new organisation properly, and rebuild the trust you let slide
Keep sitting on the fence and coasting

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: You agreed to all of it. The client is pleased for now, the plan is wrecked, and quality on the original features is starting to slip. Encouraged, the client keeps 'mentioning in passing' more work, and the scope creep has no end in sight.

options.text: Stop it now: tell the client and your manager where things stand, and reset scope and change control
Keep taking whatever comes, and have the team work late to carry it

title: Whistleblowing on your manager's fake numbers
situation: You warn your manager privately first. They deny it, then try to pull you in to 'keep it contained', even hinting it would be 'in your interest to be sensible'. You see they have no plan to stop and want you implicated too. It is messier than you thought.

options.text: Refuse to join in, keep the evidence, and report through proper channels
Give in to the pressure and inducements, and help cover it up

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: You stay off the stage and at your table, chatting and clapping along. You are still very much part of the evening. Then the table turns on Jordan, a new joiner who hates this sort of thing, and they go bright red.

options.text: Get Jordan off the hook: steer the attention elsewhere and give them a way out
Leave them to deal with it

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: InfoSec opens an investigation. Your call records with Felix are pulled.

options.text: Cooperate with the investigation
Deny it

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
situation: Your manager is put out: “Fine. Aurora is one name short.” He calls you ungrateful. Aurora goes on to win.

options.text: Put your head down and let next quarter’s delivery speak
Ask HR anonymously whether naming people who did not contribute is allowed

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: You shove the report in a drawer and keep working long weeks. Three months later, late at night on overtime, you get a violent bout of palpitations and tingling hands. A colleague takes you to A&E. The doctor is blunt: 'Keep this up and next time it will not be a warning.' Lying on the trolley, you start to do the sums again.

options.text: Take the scare seriously: stop work for a full course of treatment and rest
Once discharged, decide you are fine and dive into the next high-pressure programme

title: Who owns your side-project algorithm?
situation: The filing goes through, and you are named as inventor. Being named does not make you the owner of the patent. Once the technical detail is inside the company, your product team folds it into a core product, and the standalone product never gets off the ground. Legal then asks you to agree a separate restriction on related work after you leave. Whether that restriction would hold is a separate que

options.text: Accept it, and put your energy into a new technical direction
Negotiate a waiver of the restrictive covenant, or compensation, for after you leave

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
situation: You suggest splitting into small-group practice plus a few full run-throughs. It saves a lot of time, people stop staying late every night, and the organiser is grateful. Close to the party they have a family problem and ask whether you can take the last rehearsals and the on-the-night logistics.

options.text: Step up, run the last rehearsals and the night itself, and get the number on stage cleanly
Decline the lead: “I’ll keep rehearsing, but I’m not running the thing”

title: The client praises a feature you did not build
situation: In the Cedar Retail project review, the client’s procurement director says: “This real-time stock sync can forecast next week’s bestsellers. That’s ahead of the market.” What you actually shipped is next-day (T+1) batch sync, and forecasting is on next year’s roadmap. Kim, the product manager, catches your eye. Your manager smiles and nods. The review is going smoothly, and about £80,000 of the co

options.text: Say in the room that what is live is next-day sync, and forecasting is a later proposal
Keep quiet in the room and clarify in writing after the meeting
Stay silent and let the review pass

title: Palpitations after weeks of overtime: whether to stop
situation: You finish by pushing through, but the palpitations keep coming back over the next few days. You start to feel rattled.

options.text: Get checked straight away and make yourself keep a proper sleep routine
Tell yourself you are just tired and keep going round the clock

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
situation: Ethan guesses you know and presses for detail. HR starts looking into who knew early.

options.text: Admit you overheard, but say you did not name the list
Help Ethan understand the consultation and how to prepare for it

title: Thanking a colleague from the next team who went out of their way
situation: Last week a nasty bug in a barely maintained legacy submodule had you stuck for two days. Chris, a senior engineer on the next team, sat at your desk for a whole afternoon and helped you find and fix it. Nobody required them to spend that long. It is Friday, and you want to say thank you. You could take them out for a good lunch on you, around £30–40. You could write a formal recognition note on t

options.text: Take them out for lunch privately, straight away
Write a formal recognition note and copy their manager
Do nothing special for now and help them next time they need it

title: Load-test results clash with what product expected
situation: On launch day the system wobbles at peak. The client complains.

options.text: After the incident, admit you were pressured into fudging the load test
Call it unexpected traffic

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: In the quarterly anonymous team survey you left specific suggestions about your manager's style, including some criticism. Afterwards they tell the team that 'anonymous feedback is cowardly — if there's a problem you should say it to my face'. A few days later they take you aside: 'I don't know who it was, but I think you're the most likely to have written those detailed points. I'd like to hear w

options.text: Own it, walk through the feedback in person, and offer constructive suggestions
Deny it, suggest other possible sources, and protect the anonymity

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
situation: Their owner thanks you for the private heads-up, admits it was an oversight, and is willing to change the design. They add, offhand: "Let's keep this between us — no need to air it in the channel, or it will look as if our review missed it." You need to decide whether to share the finding with the wider teams so others can learn from it.

options.text: Agree the fix in the 1:1, then record the problem and the decision in the design doc
Anonymise it as a "performance review lesson" and share it with both teams

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You suggest that from now on every requirement goes through a rough prototype and written sign-off. The client agrees: “That would actually make this much clearer.” You also agree a sensible scope for the first rework. The team still worries that endless changes will wreck the timeline and morale.

options.text: Build sign-off and a change log into the process to protect both the client and the team
Fix how you communicate, ignore the timeline, and just work longer hours

title: Company-wide AI tools, and the fear of being replaced
situation: You nod along and barely use the new tools, working the old way. A few months later, colleagues who took up the tools are out-producing you, and even new starters using them quickly match your volume. People quietly start asking whether you are value for money. Staying as you are is now risky.

options.text: Drop the prejudice, learn the tools and rethink where your value lies
Stay stubborn and bet the company fad will pass

title: Empty your savings for a deposit, or keep cash in case work goes wrong
situation: You hold off and watch. Renting while you wait costs money, but you keep a buffer and decisions feel calmer. You feel a brief pang when family compare postcodes, but it is only a feeling and says nothing about you. Six months later both the options and your thinking have changed.

options.text: With stronger finances and a clearer head, buy without rushing when the time is right
Let worry about rising prices push you into chasing a place that does not suit you

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
situation: The personal project slows down. Colleagues notice how careful you are, and it quietly counts in your favour in the team. Someone in HR mentions in passing that they are reviewing personal use of kit, and that your approach is worth a look.

options.text: Join the review and share how you keep work and personal kit separate
Keep your head down. You don't need to preach about a personal choice

title: A request to swap on-call over a peak trading bank holiday
situation: The bank-holiday on-call rota is out. Owen has a family matter and wants to swap with you. That would put you on cover for the three highest-risk days of the break in a row, during peak trading, when alerts are much more likely. Taking it would really help the team, and Owen would owe you. But three days straight means you cannot leave town, and it will drain you. You could decline and ask your ma

options.text: Take the consecutive shifts and cover the three peak-trading days
Decline the swap and ask your manager to rebalance by the rules

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
situation: In a routine review you find a potential security hole: under certain conditions, an attacker could reach another user's data. Fixing it means rebuilding the core authorisation module. That touches much of the system, needs a long round of testing, and will probably delay a release that is about to go out. Security rates it medium: fix it soon, but don't block the release. Product is firmly agains

options.text: Block the release until the hole is fully fixed and has passed a security audit
Accept a later fix, but put temporary mitigations and monitoring in first

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
situation: A few rounds into the Christmas party, Will, usually quiet, is loudly tearing into the department and is close to marching off to ‘have it out’ with your manager. Nobody else can get through to him. He is a decent person having a bad night. If this continues he will hate himself in the morning, and the scene will be ugly. You are standing closest.

options.text: Steer him out, half-coaxing, half-supporting, and get him home with someone to look after him
Stay and watch, joining the crowd treating it as entertainment
Get well away so none of it lands on you, and leave him to it

title: Balancing a promising idea against delivery pressure
situation: You have spotted a new technical approach that could make the system much more efficient, but checking whether it works would take two to three weeks. The current sprint is already full, and your manager is clear that 'delivery commitments are non-negotiable'. You could explore it in your own time, which is slower and leaves you without the team's support, or ask to reshuffle sprint priorities, wh

options.text: Ask for 20% of the sprint to explore, and commit to dropping it if there is no breakthrough in two weeks
Explore in your own time, and only ask for formal resource once you have early results

title: Whether to tell your manager about a health problem
situation: A follow-up appointment confirms a health problem that needs a course of treatment and will sap your energy. You cannot decide whether to tell your manager. If you say something, you worry you will be treated differently and kept off important work. If you say nothing, you worry about pushing through and dropping the ball.

options.text: Tell your manager, tactfully, that you need a lighter load for a while and will keep quality up
Tell nobody. Treat it quietly and push through

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
situation: HR pass on “please set dates more clearly” to Chris. He tries two weeks of stand-ups to fix it.

options.text: Acknowledge the improvement in the meeting so that it sticks
Wait and see

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
situation: Late at night in the office you catch a department lead in a clearly intimate moment with someone who reports to them — well beyond a normal working relationship. That manager is currently reviewing the report's promotion pack, and has just changed their reporting line 'to develop them more closely'. Policy does not ban workplace relationships, but it does require a conflict-of-interest declaratio

options.text: Raise it anonymously with HR as a conflict-of-interest risk and ask them to look into it
Say nothing. It is their private life, and you have no hard evidence

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
situation: The side project keeps growing. An investor approaches you about funding an 'enterprise' direction. That would raise its value sharply and put you squarely in the company's market.

options.text: Turn the investment down, disclose the side project in full, and ask compliance to review it
Take the investment and prepare to leave, to put your energy into the side project

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: Your manager appears to accept the denial, but their expression says otherwise. Later, chances that would have been yours go to other people. The explanation is that 'others need more stretch'.

options.text: Find a better moment and admit you denied it to protect how anonymous feedback is meant to work
Live with it, let the work speak, and trust time to clear the misunderstanding

title: Stuck on the ladder: move into management or go deeper?
situation: You think both paths through. The specialist track is narrow, but the top of it is valuable. Management is wider, but it is a different job. Weighed against your temperament and how this company works, the choice becomes clearer. Now you have to act on it.

options.text: Commit: either go for a management role, or go deep enough to gain real technical influence
Finish the analysis but stay on the fence, unwilling to commit

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: Finance clears your claim quickly. Colleagues notice the total is well below what people usually claim and rib you over lunch: 'A bit too honest, aren't you? You've left money on the table.'

options.text: Say it is your own choice, and remind people what the policy actually allows
Smile it off. Keep your own standard without commenting on anyone else's

title: Your company is acquired and the culture flips
situation: A larger company buys yours, and reporting lines, processes and culture all have to fall in line with theirs. Everything you knew is changing. Some people are already leaving, and others are watching anxiously. The new owner’s rules and pace still feel foreign. With this much changing, where do you stand?

options.text: Learn how the new organisation works and where the openings are, adapt, and find where you still add value
Cling to the old culture, resist the new rules, and keep saying how much better it used to be
Play the chaos, commit to nobody, and wait to see who wins

title: Health check returning the wrong status
situation: Your load-balancer health-check endpoint returns 200, but the body says status is degraded, so traffic still hits unhealthy instances.

options.text: Fix the endpoint now and check the other services
Fix this service only
Leave it for on-call

title: A colleague rushed to hospital: a warning for you
situation: A colleague around your age, who also works late as a habit, is rushed into hospital. The news hits the team hard. Your stomach drops, because you have been living the same way.

options.text: Rebuild your sleep and exercise routine, and start actively managing your health
Feel shaken for a bit, then get busy and forget
Use the moment to start a team conversation about cutting pointless overtime

title: Vaping at the neighbouring desk
situation: After lunch, Robin at the next desk is vaping again. The cloud hangs over the open plan. The office rule is no vaping inside. You were hoping to concentrate this afternoon.

options.text: Smile and quietly remind him vaping inside isn't allowed and the shelter is downstairs
Frown and put up with it without saying anything
Post a snide note in the channel: "some people might show a bit of consideration"

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
situation: The rise puts an end to the idea of leaving. What actually bothered you, such as having no room to grow, is still there. A few months later the dissatisfaction is back. More awkwardly, the team has a rough idea that you nearly left and were bought back.

options.text: Face the real issue: discuss your career path with your manager so that staying changes something
Muddle on, and let your attitude sour

title: Colleagues invite you on a self-funded conference trip
situation: Before you leave, a colleague suggests upgrading the hotel and adding a business visit. That would take you well over your budget cap.

options.text: Stick to your budget and goals, and skip the upgrade
Say yes to keep in with the group, and worry about the money later

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
situation: Production has a critical fault and needs an immediate hotfix. The standard path of code review, staging checks and a confirmed rollback would take about two hours. A client is in the middle of a live promotional stream, and every minute of downtime is a serious loss. The operations lead hints you could ship now and backfill the process later.

options.text: Stick to the full process, and turn on a degraded mode to limit the impact on the client
Ship on a shortened path while the team prepares a rollback and completes the review within an hour

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
situation: You have decided to leave. When you get to the paperwork, HR produces a new restriction: for a year after you go, you must not join a competitor, in return for a monthly payment. Your better offer is from a company that may or may not count as a competitor. You can read the clause and negotiate, or you can decline it. The company cannot refuse a resignation you are entitled to make. The normal pos

options.text: Read the clauses, take advice if needed, and decide only once you know the scope and payment
Sign cheerfully so the exit goes smoothly, and worry about the next job later
Decline the new restriction outright

title: Balancing a promising idea against delivery pressure
situation: The request is approved. Some of the team are unhappy: their work is also queued, so why do you get time? Two weeks later the idea is technically viable, but the implementation is more complex than expected and needs more time.

options.text: Be open about the extra complexity, and ask the team to decide whether it is worth continuing
Promise to finish the implementation yourself, without team time, in return for permission to keep going

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
situation: When you come back, colleagues have covered your work and the plan has been moved around your absence. Meanwhile, someone who gritted it out to the end was admitted to hospital with acute anxiety. You can talk about what happened, or keep the details private.

options.text: If you want to, talk about the leave, and suggest the team builds a workload and support check into how it works
Keep it quiet, and prove yourself again through delivery

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: Former colleague Felix has moved to Helios. He once referred you into this job. Over dinner he asks, "Has Lynx locked the team merger yet? What's the Polaris budget?" His contract forbids him from fishing for commercial information from people who still work here.

options.text: Refuse, and keep the chat to personal matters
Share non-confidential industry gossip
Tell him about the draft merger plan, as a way of repaying the favour

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: Close to delivery, at a regular meeting, the client 'mentions in passing' three new requirements: 'These shouldn't be hard. Just do them at the same time.' In fact the change is a big one. It would squeeze the current plan and hurt quality. Their tone is casual, as if it is obviously included. Everyone in the room is watching how you respond.

options.text: Neither accept nor refuse in the meeting, and promise an impact assessment and proposal afterwards
Afraid of annoying them, agree to all of it on the spot
Refuse there and then: 'It's not in the contract. We can't do it'

title: A former colleague asks you for internal company material
situation: A former colleague gets in touch, very friendly, and asks a "small favour": send them some internal material or data. "You've got it to hand. It's not a big deal." The material is company property and covered by confidentiality. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, explain it is confidential company property that can't go outside, and keep things civil
Send the internal material because you feel you can't say no
Send it, plus extra they didn't ask for, to look generous

title: Should you leave the company a bad Glassdoor review?
situation: You have a stack of grievances and fancy leaving a low score and a rant on Glassdoor, as a warning for the next person and a chance to get it off your chest.

options.text: If you write, stick to facts: no exaggeration, no confidential detail, no personal attacks
Write a long, emotional recap of every grievance, including unverified claims
Hold off, and use the frustration to decide properly whether to stay or go

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: You helped and said your piece. Dave agreed, then 'forgot' the next time and dumped the work on you again. In front of your manager he breezily called it 'something we always do together', blurring who did what. You realise a spoken agreement means nothing to him.

options.text: Record what you help with in messages and ticket notes so credit is traceable, and reset the split
Leave it. It's less hassle to keep helping

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You rework the lot without pinning down what went wrong. Their spoken requests stay vague, and version two is sent back as well. The team is exhausted, so are you, and the real problem is still there: nothing is clearly signed off.

options.text: Stop the blind rework and put a proper sign-off in place before going further
Keep reworking on demand, exactly as they say

title: The gym after work, or staying late to get ahead
situation: You started going to the gym after work and have kept it up. You feel better and have more energy. Tonight there is a non-urgent piece of work that would make tomorrow easier if you finished it. You can only do one: the gym or staying late.

options.text: Go to the gym as planned and get the work done efficiently tomorrow
Skip the gym, stay late, and clear the work tonight
Try to do both: gym first, then stay up late to finish the work

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: In the weekly team meeting you present this quarter's reliability and performance work. Your manager listens and says, mildly, “This is basically just engineering work. If it runs, that's enough. It won't add much business value. Everyone knows that.” A few colleagues look at their screens and the room goes awkward. You know the work directly underpins the SLA on the core path, and it has real val

options.text: Politely challenge that framing on the spot, with data and business impact
Let it go in the meeting and speak to your manager afterwards
Let it pass in the room, then privately encourage colleagues and spell out what the work achieved

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
situation: The basic document goes out, but the team still comes to you for anything complicated. You are seen as the busy expert, and you turn into the bottleneck. A critical incident hits while you are on holiday, and you cannot respond in time. A fix that should have taken an hour takes six, and a customer complains.

options.text: Own the mistake, start a full write-up at once, and train a deputy
Blame the lack of a backup process, and say it wasn't entirely your fault

title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
situation: Their production system starts throwing errors, and the client complains to your manager.

options.text: Restore v2 in a hurry and review how you communicated
Insist they brought it on themselves

title: A live demo blows up in front of the client
situation: You switch to the fallback without fuss, finish the core flow, and use it to talk through the system's fault-tolerance. The client even thinks you were well prepared. After the demo their engineering lead asks you privately what caused the error.

options.text: Give the root cause straight, and promise a write-up of the investigation and fix afterwards
Fudge it: 'Small issue, doesn't affect anything'

title: How thorough to be in code review as the team grows
situation: Since the team expanded, the weekly review queue has jumped from five or six PRs to more than thirty. As technical owner, you are the named reviewer on most of the critical modules. Each PR now takes 30–40 minutes; one or two hours a day disappear into review. A new colleague's PR is in your queue: the logic is sound, but there are plenty of nits: style, edge cases, naming. You need to decide how

options.text: Review line by line and list every improvement
Focus on core logic and risk, and leave the nits to the author

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
situation: You get Will out before he does it in front of your manager. He is sick in the cab and, before he blacks out, mumbles a thanks. The next day he is mortified, and asks privately whether he made a scene and whether anyone senior saw.

options.text: Tell him the truth: it never reached your manager, and suggest he watch his drinking next time
Turn it into a story and tell it round the office in full colour

title: Whether to join a cross-team architecture review — and how hard to push
situation: You go in deep and raise a core objection to one design: they plan to introduce a framework that has not been used at scale inside the company, which carries a maintenance risk. Their owner disagrees in the meeting, fairly bluntly. The chair suggests you carry on the discussion afterwards. You need to decide what to do next.

options.text: Write a full risk assessment and submit it formally to the tech committee
Defer to their judgement and file your comments as an appendix

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: You took the lot again. At the month-end review your own work is unfinished and your manager pulls you up on it, while Dave is praised for 'on-time delivery' of work you produced. The unfairness and the performance pressure hit you at the same time.

options.text: Give your manager the facts on how the work was really split, and redraw the line
Swallow it. A falling-out is not worth it

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: Dave was put out by the gentle no that day, but then did the work himself. A week later he hits something that really is beyond him and hesitates to ask you. You hear about it.

options.text: Tell him, 'If you're really stuck, come to me', and help without doing it for him
Keep your distance. You are done being used as spare capacity

title: A colleague's clutter takes over the aisle
situation: Leon, who sits next to you, hoards things. Boxes, parcels and gym kit are all over the floor and have slowly taken over the shared aisle between you. You have to turn sideways to get past, and it is a trip hazard. He doesn't seem to see a problem.

options.text: Tell him the aisle is too tight and suggest sorting the clutter together
Squeeze past every day and say nothing
While he is away, pile all of it onto his desk

title: Desk politics in the new office
situation: You end up by a noisy walkway. Two weeks in, you are clearly finding it harder to concentrate, and you start to regret not arguing.

options.text: Ask to move, backing your case with numbers on how the desk affects your delivery
Keep putting up with it, and rely on earplugs

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: Dual-write means building a sync-and-check tool this week, which pushes out a request from the rewards centre.

options.text: Take it on and ask your manager to drop the other work
Refuse to build the tool, and force a straight choice between delaying and rushing

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: The Christmas party is in full swing. The host spots you, and your table, colleagues and manager included, starts chanting for you to get up and do something to “get the room going.” You have nothing prepared and this is not your sort of thing, but every eye is on you and someone is already holding out a microphone.

options.text: Take it in good humour: a quick gag or a bit of audience interaction, just enough to lift the room
Smile and say, ‘Thanks, but not tonight’
Shut it down flat with “I’m not doing that”, and let the room go quiet

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: Your manager asks you each to write a one-page case for attending, and a director will decide. You both get to work on it. The atmosphere is awkward but still civil.

options.text: Keep the one-pager to business value and what you would bring back, without knocking Jo
Compare the two of you in the one-pager and imply you are the better fit

title: Who picks up the bill at a client lunch
situation: You have taken a client out for a work lunch. As it winds down they say, "Let me get this," and make a move for the bill. This is ordinary client entertaining, so your side is meant to pay. How do you handle the moment?

options.text: Having already paid quietly at the desk, say, "This one's on us. You can host next time"
Wrestle over the bill at the table until it gets awkward
Go along with it and let the client pay

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
situation: The full process takes three hours. The client's live event is badly hit. The sales VP asks openly whether engineering's response time matches what the business needs. The wash-up shows the degraded mode did not fully cover the missing function.

options.text: In the wash-up, admit the process was too rigid, and propose a graded response for future emergencies
Stress quality first, and point out that a hotfix introducing a new fault would have cost more

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: The director reads both one-pagers and picks whoever fits the brief better. If you go, Jo will only half accept it. If you don't, you still need to handle it well.

options.text: If you go, offer to take turns next time. If not, help Jo get ready
Take the win or the loss and put nothing more into the relationship

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
situation: Leo is pulled in early and takes it badly. Your manager finds your name in the chat history.

options.text: Apologise and accept the reprimand
Say Sonya tricked it out of you

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
situation: Harvey is named acting lead and puts you on weekend on-call.

options.text: Take the on-call and keep the relationship
Refuse and draw a line

title: Burnout, and the urge to coast
situation: You are exhausted, and one thought keeps coming back: pack it in and just coast. It is a classic sign of burnout, and decisions made on impulse now are the ones people regret. How do you deal with it?

options.text: Take it seriously: a few days' annual leave, a saner pace, and a workload talk with your manager if needed
Bottle it, pretend you are fine, and keep running on empty
Give in to the urge to coast and start phoning the work in

title: Seated with a senior leader at the Christmas party
situation: You are too tense to speak, and you spend a rare evening at that table staring at your plate. They have no impression of you at all, and the table files you as someone who cannot open up. The chance was in front of you and you did not take it.

options.text: Catch them before people leave and introduce yourself briefly, enough to leave a decent impression
Stay silent until it is over, and miss the whole evening

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
situation: Hale, a newly hired group VP, tours the Lynx floor, stops at your desk and asks how the payments circuit breaker works. You talk for ten minutes. Afterwards colleagues mutter about whether your manager is being replaced and whether you are about to shoot up the ladder. Tara turns polite and distant. Chris is suddenly unusually courteous to you.

options.text: Brief Chris on Hale's questions and your answers
Don't make a fuss, and keep delivering as normal
Quietly take Hale's team out to lunch to build on the impression

title: Your annual bonus falls short, and you go to your manager
situation: You get the rules straight, then talk it through calmly. Your manager explains this year’s calculation, and along the way you find a place where your contribution really was undervalued. The conversation stays civil. What matters now is what you ask for next.

options.text: Show with facts what was undervalued, and push for a correction or a catch-up in next year’s rating or pay review
Hear the explanation, feel too awkward to push, and let it go

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
situation: In a team brainstorm you suggest a design, but it gets little attention. Two weeks later a colleague pitches almost the same idea in a wider meeting, with some of the same wording. A VP likes it and asks them to lead it. You cannot tell whether they got there independently or borrowed yours. Either way, they are now seen as the person who proposed it and will take most of the credit.

options.text: Speak to them privately afterwards, mention the discussion two weeks ago, and check where the idea came from
Share your earlier thinking with the team, without directly challenging their claim to the idea

title: The promotion only comes if you move into leading people: take it?
situation: A promotion is on the table, but the condition is a move into leading people. Pay and level go up, but you would largely leave hands-on engineering behind. It is the fork most engineers reach, where promotion means management. What do you decide?

options.text: Think through whether you are suited to leading people and actually want it, then decide
Fix on the pay and the title and say yes, regardless of whether it fits
Turn the promotion down without thinking, because change frightens you

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
situation: Submissions for the department’s annual Breakthrough Award close tonight. Your manager sends you the Aurora data-platform pack to look over. You have been on Lynx Payments the whole time. The team next door delivered Aurora, and you only turned up to the kick-off. Your manager messages: “I’ve added you to the list to make the bench look stronger for the panel. Just sign it.”

options.text: Ask that the pack name only those who did the work, or limit your line to the kick-off
Sign it quietly and treat it as a favour from your manager
Suggest submitting Lynx Payments instead, with you as the lead author

title: The company wants you full-stack — depth or breadth?
situation: The company wants people to go 'full-stack' and be able to pick up anything. Your strength is depth in one area, and now you are being asked to spread out. How you balance depth against breadth will shape what you end up good at.

options.text: Keep your depth as the base and widen out deliberately, building a T-shaped profile
Learn a bit of everything, master none, and lose the depth you already had
Refuse to widen out, stick to your small patch, and turn down anything new

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
situation: The project goes live. After the drinks, your body gives a louder warning: a tight chest, palpitations and a trip to A&E. The doctor says it is a physical reaction to long-running anxiety and that you need to stop. Your manager visits with news: the company wants to make you Tech Lead, if you can show you can handle the pressure.

options.text: Be honest about your health, ask to delay the promotion, and request a move onto a steadier product
Promise to get back on form, take the promotion, and keep the counselling from the team

title: Burnt out on the same work: reshape the job or not?
situation: You think it through. Is it the lack of challenge, no sense of purpose, or the feeling that you are not learning anything new? Once that is clear, you sketch out changes: automating the repetitive work, taking on a harder brief, or stretching into a neighbouring skill. You take a proposal to your manager.

options.text: Go after harder work that stretches you, and turn the burnout into a step up
Lose your nerve with the plan in hand, and back off

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: Your manager papers over it, but the client is not satisfied. Your manager asks why you did not explain in the room.

options.text: Reply to the email at once with the facts, and take ownership of the fixes
Excuse it as "not the moment to speak"
